<reason>CON built a layered case (technology already fixes checkout stigma, phase-out tiers can dissolve cliffs, universal funding dilutes the deepest need) and then converted PRO's own concessions into leverage: PRO's admission that aggregate eligibility data still must be collected undercut the admin-savings claim, and PRO's refusal to commit that summer feeding, breakfast, or food quality would be protected ("budgets aren't infinite," "a matter of how a legislature prioritizes") let CON reframe the entire debate as an unfunded promise bought at the expense of the neediest child. CON's closing crystallized this cleanly ("redistribution upward"), while PRO's closing never returned to answer the money-commitment evasion, effectively ceding CON's most decisive hit. PRO's stigma and durability arguments were reasonable but partially neutralized: cashless lines already solve visible stigma without requiring universalism, and PRO's "squeezed vs. cut" durability framing never addressed CON's point that a squeezed universal tray disproportionately harms the child with no fallback while still subsidizing families who don't need it. Both sides asked sharp, well-formatted pressure questions and answered them with proper A1/A2 labeling, so execution on that front was even; CON's rebuttal-1 being clipped is a minor cost but the core arguments still landed before the cutoff.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q2 pressing PRO to commit that no funds would come from summer feeding/breakfast/quality, and PRO's evasive answer ("budgets aren't infinite... a legislative choice"), which CON then used in Rebuttal 2 and Closing to reframe the cost objection as unrebutted.</best_rebuttal>
